head:
Health · Teenagers

Teenagers: the generation that no longer moves

Between the ages of 11 and 17, the World Health Organization (WHO) asks for 60 minutes of activity a day. Over a week, that is nearly three times what it asks of an adult, and most young people do not reach it. This article follows a single question, from the global picture to the limits of the evidence: how far short do they fall, since when, and what difference does it make once they are adults?

The problem

You have probably heard that "young people move less than they used to" or that "teenagers spend their lives on their phones". These sentences are repeated so often that they no longer say anything. Less than before, by how much? And does it matter?

To answer, we need a reference point. The WHO gives one: at least 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity for 11-17 year olds.1,2 That is the bar. So the first thing to check is simple: what share of teenagers clear it, and is that figure changing?

The second thing is trickier. An activity deficit at 15 only matters if it leaves a trace. Either young people catch up later, or they carry with them a habit, a level of fitness and a health risk. Studies that follow the same people for decades exist, but they rarely measure what we would like them to measure. So at each step we will separate what is measured from what is assumed.

The question

Do teenagers move clearly less than the WHO recommends, since when, and does this deficit follow them into adulthood?

The demonstration runs in six steps, from the broadest to the most precise: the global picture, the slope with age, the case of France, persistence into adulthood, the health consequences, then the objections. The answer comes afterwards, with the level of certainty of each piece.

What is at stake

What is at stake is first read in the list the WHO itself gives. In children and adolescents, physical activity is associated with better physical fitness and better cardiometabolic health, stronger bones, better cognitive outcomes and better mental health, less body fat, healthy muscle development and better motor skills.3 These are associations: the WHO page does not say, for each one, how much is causal.

The second stake is time. A habit is formed, reinforced or lost at an age when you rarely decide for yourself: school, family, timetables and means of transport decide for you. At 25, you choose. At 14, others often choose for you, and what you learn to do with your body at that time becomes your starting point. This is reasoning, not a study result, but step 4 will test part of it.

The third stake is an inequality: we will see that girls lag further behind boys in almost every country.

The last stake concerns tests. A physical fitness test measures what the body has become after months of movement or sedentary behaviour, not the week's activity. Knowing where you stand is only useful if you know what that level foretells and what you can expect by changing it: that is what we try to pin down here, without promising more than the figures allow.

Step 1 of 6 · The global picture

The age at which the most movement is asked for is an age at which the majority do not reach the bar

Let us start with what is asked. The WHO recommends that adults do at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity activity.3 For 11-17 year olds, the bar is 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity.1,2 Over seven days, that makes 420 minutes. That is my own calculation (60 times 7), not a published figure: the recommendation is daily and the intensities are not identical.

The recommendation is nearly three times higher at 11-17 than in adulthood

Adult: weekly minimum of moderate-intensity activity (WHO). Teenager: 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous intensity, multiplied by 7: derived figure, the two intensities are not equivalent. Sources: WHO, Guthold et al. 2020.1,3

What this means

At this age, the threshold is far more demanding than for an adult. The WHO associates activity in this period with stronger bones and healthy muscle development.3 The higher the bar, the more it costs to fall below it: let us look at where young people stand.

The largest analysis available pooled 298 school-based surveys from 146 countries and territories, covering 1.6 million students aged 11 to 17, between 2001 and 2016. Result for 2016: 81.0% of students did not reach 60 minutes (uncertainty interval 77.8 to 87.7). Among boys, 77.6%; among girls, 84.7%.1 This 81% figure is the one you read everywhere. It does come from there: Guthold and colleagues, in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health, in 2020, with funding from the WHO.

In fifteen years, the share of teenagers below the bar has barely moved

Share of students aged 11 to 17 below 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day. The two grey bars are 2001, the coloured ones 2016. Uncertainty interval for the overall figure in 2016: 77.8 to 87.7. Source: Guthold et al., The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health, 2020.1

What this means

If we flip the figure, 19 teenagers in 100 reach the bar (100 minus 81, simple calculation). Among girls, about 15 in 100. Between 2001 and 2016, the share below the bar fell from 80.1% to 77.6% among boys, a fall judged statistically significant, and from 85.1% to 84.7% among girls, a change the authors do not judge significant.1 In fifteen years, no catching up: the problem is not a recent fashion, it is a lasting state of affairs.

Two clarifications make this finding sturdier than a single figure. The gap between girls and boys is 7.1 points (84.7 minus 77.6), and girls are less active than boys in every country in the study except four out of 146; in 27 countries, at least 90% of girls are below the bar, against two countries for boys.2 And there is no clear link with the country's wealth: low-income countries (84.9%) and high-income countries (79.4%) do not stand apart in any clear pattern.1

So we know that most do not clear the bar, not when it matters. To know that, we have to follow the same children over time.

Step 2 of 6 · The slope with age

The decline does not start in adolescence: it starts in childhood

To see a slope, we need a repeated objective measurement in the same people. The Gateshead Millennium Study cohort, in north-east England, provides one: 545 children wore an accelerometer for five to seven days at ages 7, 9, 12 and 15.4 An accelerometer does not record what the child says they did: it records movement. That is the difference from the questionnaire surveys of step 1.

On average, minutes of activity fall below the 60-minute bar, then keep declining

Minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity, measured by accelerometer, group average at each age (545 children, 217 measured at all four ages). The average is not the share of children who reach the bar. Source: Farooq et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018.4

What this means

From 7 to 15, the boys' average falls from 75.5 to 51.4 minutes a day, that is 24.1 minutes less; the girls' from 63.4 to 41.0, that is 22.4 minutes less. In proportion, that is about a third less (32% and 35%, my own calculation). Girls drop below the 60-minute line by age 9 on average, boys around age 12. In other words, at 15 a teenager does on average about two thirds of what they did at 7 (51.4 out of 75.5 and 41.0 out of 63.4): the gap is not created all at once.

The authors also looked at whether the decline accelerates in adolescence, as is often believed. They conclude that it does not: all trajectories decline from age 7, and they find no evidence that the decline is steeper in adolescence, or steeper in girls than in boys.4 The only exception: 19% of boys stayed at a high and stable level between 7 and 15. Among girls, no trajectory stays at a high and stable level.4

Two cautions. The first: an average below 60 minutes does not say that every child is below 60. It is likely that many are, but the average alone does not prove it. The second: this is a cohort from one region of England, representative of its population in socio-economic terms, not of France.4 So we need to look at what happens here.

Step 3 of 6 · The case of France

In France, the drop happens at the start of adolescence, and it continues among girls

The French data come from three sources that do not measure quite the same thing, and it is important to say so from the outset. The Esteban study (2014-2016), taken up by Santé publique France and by the Observatoire national de l'activité physique et de la sédentarité (ONAPS), gives the share of 6-17 year olds who reach the WHO recommendation: 50.7% of boys and 33.3% of girls.5,6 Broken down by age, the picture changes markedly.

In France, the share of young people reaching the bar collapses at the start of adolescence

Share of young people reaching the recommendation of 60 minutes a day, in France, Esteban study 2014-2016, as reported by ONAPS (Report Card 2020). Rounded values. Ages 6-10 are measured by a questionnaire completed by a parent, ages 11-17 by self-report questionnaire.5,7

What this means

Between ages 6-10 and 11-14, the share reaching the bar loses 36 points among boys (70 to 34) and among girls (56 to 20): that is a difference I calculate, and it is identical. The reports describe a marked drop at puberty.5,6 After that, the two sexes part ways: at 15-17, boys recover a little (40%), while girls keep declining (16%, about one in six). The lag of girls seen at the global level is found here too, and it widens with age.

The two other sources give similar orders of magnitude. According to Anses, relying on the national INCA 3 survey, only a third of 11-17 year olds do at least 60 minutes of activity a day.8 A trade press article relays the Anses expertise: 66% of 11-17 year olds do not do enough physical activity.9 The differences come from the surveys, the definitions and the age bands, not from a contradiction: all of them say that the majority is below the bar.

Over time, the finding is less clear than worldwide. Between 2006-2007 and 2014-2016, the share of young people reaching the recommendation did not change in France.7,5 On the other hand, the international HBSC survey, reported by ONAPS, shows a decline at every age between 2014 and 2018: for example, among 15-year-old girls, from 14% to 11%.5 These figures are far lower than those of Esteban (definition not detailed in the page read): we only retain the direction of change. During the first lockdown of 2020, 58.7% of teenagers reported having reduced their activity, and 68.9% reported spending more time in front of a screen.5

Screens are the explanation that comes first. The French data point in that direction, without being able to demonstrate it: the share of young people who stay under two hours of screen time a day goes, among boys, from 28.3% at 6-10 to 2.6% at 15-17, and among girls from 41.5% to 13.7%.5 Leisure screen time rose by about 20 minutes a day among 3-17 year olds between 2006-2007 and 2014-2015.8 These figures show that the two curves move in opposite directions with age. They do not show that the screen replaces movement: a teenager can do both, and between 2006-2007 and 2014-2016 the share of young people reaching the bar did not change even though screen time increased.

That leaves the question that makes all this serious or not: does the deficit disappear with the end of adolescence, or does it last?

Step 4 of 6 · Persistence into adulthood

Activity levels in childhood and youth are, for many, found again in adulthood

To know whether the deficit lasts, we have to follow people for decades. The Finnish Young Finns study did so: 3,596 people (1,764 boys and 1,832 girls) aged 3 to 18 in 1980, followed for about 31 years, with self-reported activity at ages ranging from 9 to 49.10 The researchers did not average: they looked for families of trajectories.

More than half of participants stay low-active from childhood to middle age

Distribution of the 3,596 participants across five self-reported physical activity trajectories, from 9 to 49. The percentages are those of the study and total 100%. Source: Rovio et al., The Young Finns Study, 2018.10

What this means

Only 6.6% of participants stayed active throughout, and 51.4% stayed low-active all the way through. If we add the two groups "low-active" and "inactive" (51.4 plus 14.6, my own calculation), that makes 66% of participants: two out of three were never at a high level. The habit of being sedentary is therefore not an episode of adolescence that you leave behind. But the study also shows that 13.5% of participants became more and more active: nothing is fixed.

Activity there is self-reported, not measured by a device. The group is Finnish and grew up from 1980, in an environment very different from that of a teenager today. Above all, the study describes trajectories and their determinants (education, smoking, having children): it does not demonstrate that inactivity in adolescence causes inactivity in adulthood, since both may come from the same family and social factors.10 It is enough to say that the vast majority do not "catch up".

If inactivity lasts, we still need to know what it costs. The best way to find out is to look at young people who were followed into adulthood and for whom something was measured at 18.

Step 5 of 6 · Consequences in adulthood

Fitness measured at the end of adolescence goes with health problems almost thirty years later

In Sweden, physical fitness was measured at military enlistment, between 16 and 19 years of age. Researchers at the Karolinska Institutet went back over the records of 1,079,128 men who entered the army between 1972 and 1994 and followed them for a median of 28.3 years.11 The outcome studied is the award of a disability pension, that is, lasting inability to work: it happened to 54,304 of them (about 5%, my own calculation).

Beware of a nuance that structures this whole step: what is measured at enlistment is cardiorespiratory fitness (tested on a bike), not the amount of activity. The two are linked, but not identical: fitness also depends on genetics and growth. I have not read here a study that quantifies what share of fitness at that age comes from the movement of the preceding years. The link with activity is therefore plausible, not demonstrated by these sources.

Low fitness between 16 and 19 goes with an almost fourfold higher risk, comparable to that of severe obesity

Risk ratio (hazard ratio) for a disability pension, Swedish men followed for almost 30 years from the age of 16-19. The first two are published (3.74, interval 3.55 to 3.95; 3.21, interval 2.49 to 4.15). The last two are derived, calculated as the inverse of 0.28 and of 0.26 (high fitness versus low), for a different outcome (pension for cardiovascular disease): to be read as an order of magnitude, the interval for heart failure is wide (0.10 to 0.70). Sources: Henriksson et al., Annals of Internal Medicine and European Heart Journal, 2019.11,12

What this means

A hazard ratio of 3.74 means that, at a given moment of follow-up, the rate of disability pensions awarded was about 3.7 times higher in the least fit tenth than in the fittest tenth. It does not say that 3.7 times more men are disabled: only 5% were in total. What is striking is the comparison: low fitness weighs about as much as severe obesity (3.21). In the same study, the fittest men had fewer pensions in every weight category: fitness is not just a reflection of weight.11

A second analysis on the same population (1,078,685 men, 2,289 pensions for cardiovascular disease) gives detail by type of disease. For cerebrovascular disease (1,222 cases), the risk of the fittest men is 0.28 times that of the least fit (interval 0.21 to 0.37). For heart failure (147 cases), 0.26 (0.10 to 0.70). For ischaemic heart disease, the ratio is 0.11 (0.05 to 0.29), but on only 346 cases, which makes the interval very wide and the figure fragile.12 Combining low fitness and obesity at 18 gives a ratio of 7.54 for ischaemic heart disease (3.06 to 18.58): the two factors add up, and the authors conclude that prevention would benefit from starting young.12

The limits are clear: men only, little data on smoking and alcohol, and no measurement between enlistment and pension.13 It is a strong association, across more than a million people, but an observational one. This is the moment to raise the objections.

Step 6 of 6 · Objections and what remains uncertain

What holds up when we try to demolish the reasoning, and what cannot be asserted

First objection: is the 81% figure reliable? It is well sourced, but it carries caveats. The uncertainty interval runs from 77.8 to 87.7%. The data are uneven: 56 of the 75 high-income countries, but 8 of the 31 low-income countries; only 73 of the 146 countries had at least two years of data, which limits the analysis of trends.2 And the data stop in 2016: they say nothing about the effect of recent years, except for France, where the 2020 lockdown reduced the reported activity of more than half of teenagers.5 The order of magnitude is solid (the French sources, which are independent, also find a majority below the bar); the decimal is not.

Second objection: what if causality were reversed, or something else explained everything? A teenager with low fitness is perhaps also a teenager who is ill, or who comes from a background that offers fewer opportunities to move and, later, less access to care. The Swedish study accounts for body mass index, but the researchers themselves point out the lack of data on smoking and alcohol.13 In the Finnish study, the trajectories are linked to smoking, level of education and having children.10 None of these studies is a randomised trial: none proves that increasing a teenager's activity lowers their adult risk. This is the most important point of this step.

Third objection: is 60 minutes a magic threshold? No. It is a recommendation, not a cliff, and the sources read do not say from how many minutes the benefit levels off. The Finnish study also shows that 13.5% of participants improved: the habit can change.10

Fourth objection: is adolescence the time of life when people move the least? That is the implicit claim of the title, and the data read do not demonstrate it. They show that the threshold is highest at this age, that more than four in five do not reach it, and that the average declines from childhood to age 15. They do not compare the activity of teenagers with that of adults of 30 or 60. So we should retain a precise fact (a large and lasting deficit) and not the general formula.

The answer to the problem

We started from this question: do teenagers move clearly less than the WHO recommends, since when, and does this deficit follow them into adulthood?

What is solid. Yes, the great majority is below the bar: 81% worldwide in 2016; in France, about two thirds according to Anses, and between 60% and 84% depending on age and sex according to Esteban (calculated from the shares reaching the bar). Girls lag further behind boys almost everywhere. In fifteen years, nothing has changed for girls, and little for boys. These findings come from independent sources that converge on the order of magnitude.

What is probable. The decline starts in childhood, not in adolescence, at least in the cohort measured by accelerometer; in France, the break is visible at the start of adolescence. The activity level of childhood is, for many, found again in adulthood: about two out of three participants in the Finnish cohort were never at a high level. Low physical fitness between 16 and 19 goes with a markedly higher risk of cardiovascular disease and disability three decades later, at a level comparable to that of severe obesity.

What is not established. That getting a teenager to move more then reduces their adult risks: none of the studies read tests it. That fitness at 18 reflects the activity of the preceding years rather than genetics or growth: plausible, not quantified here. That adolescence is the low point of life in terms of activity. And the current situation: the global data stop in 2016.

The frank answer is therefore: yes for the deficit, yes for its duration in a large share of cases, yes for the association with health in adulthood, no for the proof that correcting the deficit at 15 is enough to change that trajectory. The title "the generation that no longer moves" is stronger than the figures: teenagers do move, but most not enough, and less and less with age.

What to put in place

What follows is ordered, and only the first part of each point rests on what we have read. Where it is an editorial choice, it is said.

  1. Measure first where you stand, on two levels.The test on this page assesses physical fitness, that is, what the body has built. It does not tell you how many minutes a day you move. Both are useful: fitness is what the Swedish study measured, minutes are what the WHO recommends. For a week, note the time you move enough to be out of breath, and compare it with 60 minutes a day on average.
  2. Aim for the bar without turning it into an obligation.If you are clearly below it, the goal is not to go from 20 to 60 minutes in a week. The average lost about 22 to 24 minutes a day between ages 7 and 15, over eight years. No study read gives the ideal progression: aiming for a few more minutes each day before aiming for 60 is an editorial choice.
  3. Vary what you do.Anses recommends promoting activity of several types, cardiorespiratory, strength training and flexibility, and counting everyday movement (walking, stairs, carrying loads).8
  4. Break up sitting time.The same opinion recommends interrupting long periods of sitting with active breaks.8 Nothing proves that the screen is the cause of the lag, but a movement break costs nothing.
  5. Pay particular attention to girls and to 11-14 year olds.This is where the data show the biggest gap: one girl in six reaches the bar at 15-17 in France, and the drop is steepest between 6-10 and 11-14. At that age, the question is not "doing sport" but "keeping up an activity you enjoy".
  6. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. This frequency is an editorial choice: none of the studies read sets it. You will see a trend, not a verdict.

Chest pain, unusual breathlessness or feeling unwell during exertion justify medical advice before increasing effort. A low score on a test is not a diagnosis: it is a starting point.

What these figures do not say
  • Studies on adulthood are observational. The Swedish ones cover only men and measure fitness, not activity.11,12,13
  • No trial read shows that increasing a teenager's activity reduces their risks in adulthood.

Frequently asked questions

Is the 81% figure the one for France?

No. It is the 2016 global figure for school-attending 11-17 year olds.1 In France, Anses counts about two thirds of 11-17 year olds below the bar, and Esteban gives 60% to 84% depending on age and sex (calculated from the shares who reach it, 16% among girls aged 15-17).5,8,9

If my teenager is under 60 minutes, is it serious?

It is not a danger threshold: it is a recommendation. It is better to look at the trend and at physical fitness than to fixate on a figure on a given day.

Can you catch up in adulthood?

In the Finnish cohort, 13.5% of participants became more and more active.10 The study does not say what effect this had on their health.
